Strategy for Supplier Screening
AIL integrates ESG considerations 
into the evaluation of new and existing Business Partners (BPs) through a risk-based screening approach. The assessment considers geopolitical exposure, sector-level risks, supplier concentration, and publicly available information, and is supported by internal reviews to enable informed decision-making and proactive risk management across the supplier lifecycle.
By embedding ESG considerations into supplier screening and onboarding, AIL establishes stronger Business Partner relationships while proactively managing operational, compliance and sustainability risks across the value chain. New Business Partners are evaluated through structured questionnaires, documentation review and due diligence before approval, ensuring that both commercial capability and ESG performance are assessed together as part of the onboarding process.
As of March 31, 2026, 100% of Business Partners had signed and committed to 
AIL’s Supplier Code of Conduct, with contractual agreements incorporating clauses on environmental protection, health and safety, labour practices and human rights. At the contracting stage, all Business 
Partners must commit to AIL’s sustainability expectations. Prior to engagement, Business Partners sign the General Conditions of Contract, General Conditions of Purchase and comply with requirements relating to health and safety, labour practices, POSH, responsible procurement and the Supplier Code of Conduct. This common framework establishes clear expectations from the outset and promotes consistent governance across every Business Partner relationship.
The Supplier Code of Conduct outlines 
AIL’s expectations across ethics, labour practices, human rights, occupational health and safety, environmental protection and regulatory compliance, providing a consistent framework for responsible business conduct throughout the supply chain.

Evaluation of Business Partners (BP)
Using a risk-based approach based on prior-year spend, AIL prioritizes key BPs for ESG due diligence. This covers engineering and trading partners exceeding `1 Cr, alongside major raw 
material and packaging suppliers selected by criticality, origin, and supply risk, focusing on suppliers with the highest operational significance and sustainability impact.
Key partners are prioritized for 
comprehensive ESG assessments covering environmental metrics, social standards, and governance parameters based on prior-year spend and operational criticality. Trading partners are also evaluated for information security.Aligned with international frameworks like EcoVadis, UNGC, ISO, TfS, and SA8000, these evaluations identify ecosystem risks and opportunities consistently with global ESG practices.

The assessment and appointment of Board members prioritise ethics, personal and professional stature, domain expertise, 
gender diversity. For Independent Directors, the criteria outlined in the Companies Act, 2013 and SEBI Listing Regulations are also taken into account. Remuneration paid to directors is within the limit approved by the shareholders. Remuneration for KMPs, SMPs, and other employees includes fixed pay, allowances, and performance-linked variable pay tied to individual, business unit, and corporate outcomes to foster a high-performance culture.
Long-term incentives are delivered via Performance Stock Options (PSOs) with annual targets set by the Nomination and 
Remuneration Committee. Vesting performance is based on a weighted average of two financial metrics: EBITDA (60% weight) and ROIC (40% weight). The NRC Committee has the authority to adjust performance targets to reflect market conditions and economic factors.
The CEO’s compensation comprises fixed pay, variable pay, and long-term incentives linked to strategic and financial 
metrics like profitability, EBITDA, and ROCE, aligning leadership with sustainable shareholder value.Nomination and Remuneration ProcessEligible directors, except for managing directors and independent directors, are required to retire by rotation. Every year, at least one-third of the directors retire by rotation and, based on their eligibility and consent, are reappointed. As per the Companies Act, 2013, each Board member is elected individually, allowing shareholders to vote on each candidate separately.Annual Election of Board Members
There are no limitations on directors’ liabilities, meaning board members are fully accountable for their actions and decisions in accordance with applicable corporate laws, fiduciary duties, and regulatory requirements. This approach reinforces a strong governance framework by promoting responsible oversight, ethical conduct, and diligence in decision-making. The absence of liability limitations serves as a safeguard to protect the interests of shareholders and other stakeholders by ensuring that directors uphold the highest standards of accountability and integrity in the performance of their duties.Director Liabilities
As part of our digital governance initiatives, we implemented a Board Meetings Management Solution during the reporting 
period. It enhanced our already well-established processes by making documentation access more seamless, improving accessibility of meeting materials, and supporting a more efficient way of working. 
The Company has a robust digital Compliance Management Tool as part of its enterprise-wide governance and risk 
management framework, enabling real-time monitoring, audit readiness and effective management of compliances across its operations. The tool includes a dedicated licence management module to monitor renewals across locations and provides automated alerts to compliance owners for timely action on statutory obligations and renewals in accordance with regulatory timelines. Compliance owners are required to submit the status of their respective obligations, which are subsequently reviewed by designated approvers to ensure accountability and oversight. A quarterly compliance status report, including corrective actions, is presented to the Board of Directors, reinforcing oversight and governance effectiveness.Digital initiatives and Compliance Tool

Targeted upskilling has enhanced leadership awareness of digital tools and AI, promoting responsible integration and technology-driven governance. Further details on employee learning are available in the Human Capital chapter. AI is systematically integrated into operational workflows. Senior leaders drive functional deployment to increase agility, with adoption metrics embedded in Key Result Areas (KRAs) to ensure executive accountability.Future-ready LeadershipAIL’s Code of Conduct establishes the organizational foundation for ethical behavior, promoting integrity, accountability, and responsible decision-making while reinforcing stakeholder trust. It mandates compliance with all laws, regulations, and internal guidelines, applying universally to all employees, associates, officers, and Directors across AIL and its subsidiaries.
By requiring personnel to prioritize the Company’s interests, safeguard its reputation, avoid conflicts, and act honestly, AIL 
strengthens an organization-wide culture of accountability, transparency, and ethical practices.The Company is built on a foundation of trust, honesty, and the highest ethical standards. We strictly adhere to all applicable laws and maintain a zero-tolerance policy for bribery, corruption, or any unauthorized personal gain influencing business decisions. This unwavering ethical framework governs all business relationships and applies universally to our internal teams—including employees and board directors—as well as external partners, consultants, vendors, agents, and any public interactions with government officials acting on our behalf.

The mechanism protects whistleblowers from retaliation, ensures confidential investigations, and implements corrective 
actions, with updates periodically reviewed by the Audit Committee and Board.

182 Integrated Annual Report 2025-26MANAGEMENT DISCUSSION AND ANAL YSIS - A YEAR OF 
‘INTEGRATED RESILIENCE’
 ECONOMIC OVERVIEW
Global Economy
The 
macroeconomic environment reflected moderate 
growth amid evolving policy, trade and geopolitical 
dynamics. According to the IMF’s World Economic Outlook, 
April 2026, global growth stabilised at 3.1%. However, this 
headline stability masked a deeper structural shift, as 
economies continued to adjust to the delayed effects of 
monetary tightening, shifting inflation trends, and a more 
policy-led global trade environment.
These conditions also influenced the global speciality 
chemicals industry. Following the prolonged inventory 
destocking cycle witnessed during 2023-25, the industry 
entered CY 2025 on a more normalised footing. As inventory 
levels stabilised across end-user industries, demand 
visibility improved selectively. This was particularly evident 
in areas linked to replacement cycles in agrochemicals 
and secular growth in high-performance polymers and 
electronics.
At the same time, global trade flows increasingly reflected 
what McKinsey describes as ‘The Great Re-shoring’. 
Industrial policy, supply security and geopolitical alignment 
became as important as cost competitiveness. Persistent 
regional tensions and evolving trade alliances gradually 
shifted corporate priorities from ‘Just-in-Time’ efficiency 
to ‘Just-in-Case’ resilience. This transition strengthened 
the relevance of dependable manufacturing partners. 
Companies such as AIL remained well-positioned as safe-
harbour partners for global MNCs seeking to de-risk supply 
chains, diversify sourcing and improve long-term continuity.
Supply-side conditions remained broadly stable, although 
intermittent geopolitical developments continued to create 
volatility in energy prices, logistics, and trade flows. In 
response, companies placed greater emphasis on supply 
chain diversification, regional partnerships and resource 
optimisation. This strengthened collaboration across 
geographies, industries, and value chains, serving as a key 
enabler of resilience and sustainable growth.
Growth trends, however, remained uneven across 
economies. Advanced markets recorded relatively subdued 
expansion amid tighter financial conditions. Meanwhile, 
emerging markets, particularly in Asia, continued to 
demonstrate resilience, supported by domestic demand, 
industrial investment, and manufacturing-led activity. 
As central banks adopted a gradual and data-dependent 
easing path, financial conditions remained relatively tight. 
This environment favoured companies with prudent capital 
allocation, healthy internal accruals and disciplined balance 
sheet management. Such strengths enabled them to pursue 
growth without compromising financial flexibility.Trade and investment engagements progressed selectively. 
Ongoing discussions involving India, including those with 
the US and the European Union, have improved medium-
term visibility into market access, export opportunities, and 
participation in global supply chains. For Indian speciality 
chemical players, this evolving environment created 
opportunities to deepen global partnerships, expand 
into higher-value applications and strengthen their role in 
resilient and diversified supply networks.

Outlook
The global economy is expected to grow at a measured 
pace, 
shaped by policy direction, financial conditions, and 
evolving trade linkages. Emerging markets are likely to 
remain supported by domestic demand and investment 
activity. However, advanced economies may witness a more 
gradual recovery as monetary conditions remain relatively 
tight. As a result, the overall growth profile is expected to 
stay uneven across regions and sectors.
Inflation is anticipated to moderate during the year. However, 
fluctuations in energy prices and shifting trade dynamics 
may lead to intermittent volatility. In this environment, 
central banks are expected to adopt a cautious and data-
dependent approach. Policy adjustments are therefore 
likely to remain gradual. Overall, the global environment is 
expected to be characterised by steady yet sensitive growth, 
with external developments and policy signals continuing to 
play a critical role.
Source: World Economic Outlook Update, April 2026
Indian Economy
India maintained its position among the fastest-growing 
major economies despite a challenging global environment. 
According to Provisional Estimates, the Real GDP growth 
rate for FY 2025-26 stood at 7.7%. Strong domestic 
demand, resilient consumption and continued public 
capital expenditure supported this momentum. These 
factors helped offset external headwinds arising from 
global trade uncertainties and financial market volatility. 
Macroeconomic fundamentals also remained stable during 
the year, supported by prudent fiscal management and a 
well-calibrated monetary policy environment.

at vision further strengthened this growth momentum. 
Policy initiatives such as the National Logistics Policy 
and PM Gati Shakti continued to improve infrastructure 
planning, logistics efficiency and multimodal connectivity. 
In parallel, investments in specialised chemical zones and 
logistics corridors are reducing the logistics cost burden 
on Indian exports. As a result, India’s competitiveness 
as a manufacturing and export-oriented economy has 
strengthened further. This is particularly relevant for sectors 
such as speciality chemicals, which depend on reliable 
infrastructure, efficient material movement and faster 
access to global markets.
Inflationary pressures remained largely contained during 
the year. Favourable agricultural output and effective 
supply-side measures, particularly across food categories, 
supported this trend. Consequently, the overall environment 
remained supportive of household consumption and 
investment activity. Against this backdrop, monetary policy 
remained data-driven. The RBI maintained a balanced 
approach between supporting growth and ensuring price 
stability.
At the same time, India’s efforts to reduce dependence on 
China for key intermediates created a significant domestic 
opportunity for import substitution. This shift is encouraging 
Indian manufacturers to build deeper capabilities across 
critical chemistries and improve backward integration. It 
is also enabling them to serve both domestic and global 
customers with greater reliability. For companies such as 
AIL, this creates a meaningful platform to support India’s 
self-reliance agenda while expanding into higher-value and 
more specialised product segments.
Trade and investment prospects also improved during the 
year. This was supported by progress in India’s Free Trade 
Agreement discussions with the United Kingdom and the 
European Union. For Indian speciality chemical companies, 
including AIL, these agreements offer opportunities beyond 
duty benefits. They can support technical collaboration, 
IP-sensitive co-development, improved market access and 
deeper integration with global value chains. Consequently, 
India’s economic resilience is increasingly being reinforced 
by stronger domestic fundamentals, policy-led infrastructure 
development, import-substitution opportunities, and 
expanding global trade partnerships.

INDUSTRY OVERVIEW
Global Chemical Industry
The 
global chemical industry entered 2026 amid subdued 
economic growth, elevated geopolitical tensions and the 
lingering effects of prolonged inventory destocking across 
several end-user sectors. Growth expectations for the global 
chemicals industry moderated from earlier projections 
as weaker industrial activity, trade uncertainty, tariffs and 
sanctions affected demand visibility and influenced long-
term sourcing strategies.
However, the industry also began moving beyond the post-
2022 cyclical correction that started in early 2023. As 
inventory levels normalised across key value chains, the 
recovery became increasingly selective rather than broad-
based. This led to the emergence of a two-speed growth 
model within the sector.
=== page 95 ===
184 Integrated Annual Report 2025-26Commodity and bulk chemicals continued to face pressure 
from overcapacity, intense competition and margin 
compression. These challenges were driven largely by 
China’s significant capacity additions over the past few 
years. The additional capacities altered global trade flows 
and created medium- to long-term competitive pressure 
across several end applications.
In contrast, speciality and knowledge-led chemicals 
demonstrated stronger resilience. Growth in these 
segments was supported by higher-value applications 
and customer-specific solutions. These segments are 
estimated to grow at nearly 1.5 times the rate of GDP growth, 
driven by structural demand from the energy transition, 
electric vehicles, semiconductor localisation, sustainable 
agriculture, electronics, high-performance polymers, and 
advanced manufacturing.
The growing need for performance-driven materials and 
application-specific solutions continued to support value-
added product categories. At the same time, traditional 
bulk chemical segments experienced relatively subdued 
demand.
These trends extended the industry’s recovery timeline 
while increasing differentiation across product categories 
and business models. Companies focused on specialised 
chemistries, customer intimacy, technical capabilities and 
innovation-led portfolios demonstrated relatively stronger 
growth and profitability. As a result, collaboration became 
increasingly central to value creation. Companies continued 
to co-develop products with customers, form strategic 
alliances and integrate across value chains to enhance 
competitiveness.In an uncertain and volatile environment, global companies 
also adopted multifold strategies to strengthen supply 
chain resilience and reduce dependence on concentrated 
sourcing ecosystems. This accelerated a shift from ‘Just-in-
Time’ efficiency to ‘Just-in-Case’ preparedness. Companies 
increasingly prioritised supplier diversification, inventory 
flexibility, regional sourcing options and long-term supply 
assurance.
This realignment received further support from China’s anti-
involution drive, which aims to curb irrational price wars 
and excessive capacity-led competition. For India, as an 
emerging alternative sourcing partner for various chemical 
products, this presents a significant opportunity to establish 
itself as a preferred global hub for chemicals and speciality 
manufacturing.
Sustainability also became a fundamental strategic priority 
for the industry. The transition towards greener and more 
circular solutions is creating a sizeable market opportunity 
for new-age chemicals, including bio-based products, 
advanced circular materials and sustainable process 
technologies.
Companies continued to accelerate investments in green 
chemistry, recycling technologies and sustainable product 
lines in response to tightening regulations and evolving 
customer preferences. At the same time, supply chain 
optimisation and strategic collaborations gained further 
importance, as industry participants worked to improve 
resilience while aligning with emerging circular economy 
principles.

Outlook
Despite cyclical challenges, structural demand drivers 
continue 
to support the chemical industry’s long-
term outlook. Demand growth remains driven by 
urbanisation, infrastructure development, electric 
mobility, semiconductors, renewable energy, healthcare, 
electronics, agriculture, and consumer goods. Speciality 
chemicals continue to demonstrate greater resilience than 
commodity chemicals. This is primarily due to higher value 
addition, customised applications, and stronger customer 
integration.
Reflecting these underlying drivers, the sector’s long-term 
outlook remains positive. According to projections from 
ACC and ICCA, the global chemical industry is expected to 
grow by 3-4%, broadly in line with overall economic activity. 
However, the growth trajectory is likely to remain uneven 
across regions and segments.
In the near term, commodity chemicals may continue to 
face pressure due to soft demand and excess capacity. 
Over the medium term, speciality chemicals are expected 
to witness stronger growth. This trend is already visible in 
sectors such as electronics, clean energy, and advanced 
manufacturing, as highlighted by McKinsey and Deloitte  
(FY 2024-25).
At the same time, shifts in global supply chains are expected 
to gradually rebalance production towards emerging hubs 
such as India. Existing manufacturing hubs, including 
those in Europe, continue to face structural disadvantages 
stemming from high energy costs. This has led to ongoing 
asset rationalisation across the region. 
Sustainability considerations, including investments in 
green chemistry and low-carbon processes, are also 
expected to play a more central role in shaping long-
term competitiveness. Overall, industry performance will 
depend on product mix, geographic positioning, and the 
ability to adapt to evolving geopolitical and environmental 
requirements.Indian Chemical Industry
The Indian chemical industry continued to demonstrate 
resilience during FY 2025-26 despite a challenging global 
environment. The sector faced demand moderation, 
overcapacity in commodity chemicals, volatile feedstock 
prices, and geopolitical uncertainties. However, strong 
domestic demand, rising export opportunities, and 
increasing supply-chain diversification continued to support 
growth. As a result, India strengthened its position as a 
strategically important manufacturing destination.
Driven by these favourable dynamics, the sector’s economic 
footprint is expanding rapidly. The industry is currently 
estimated at USD 155-165 billion and is projected to reach 
USD 230-255 billion by 2030, implying a CAGR of around 
8-9%. The sector remains highly diversified and includes 
petrochemicals, speciality chemicals, agrochemicals, 
and pharmaceuticals, amongst others. It also continues 
to contribute meaningfully to India’s industrial output and 
manufacturing value addition.
India’s speciality chemicals segment remains a key 
growth engine for the industry. Demand from automobiles, 
electronics, construction chemicals, pharmaceuticals, 
personal care, water treatment, and renewable energy 
sectors is expected to support continued investments in 
value-added downstream products.
This multi-sectoral demand for speciality chemicals has 
created a resilient manufacturing ecosystem. In turn, this 
ecosystem serves as a strong foundation for international 
expansion. Leveraging this domestic strength, India has 
positioned itself as a key alternative manufacturing hub. 
The country also stands to benefit significantly from 
the forthcoming implementation of India-UK, India-EU, 
and India-Oman FTA arrangements. Furthermore, cost 
competitiveness, a skilled workforce, and improved 
infrastructure continue to drive this shift.

Opportunities
India 
is strategically positioned to benefit from several 
structural and cyclical opportunities emerging across the

integrated and collaborative players, which offer long-

sectors. For the chemical industry, these initiatives

production. This is especially relevant for sectors 
linked to electronics, clean energy, advanced materials

1.  Geopolitical and Trade Volatility: Persistent geopolitical 
tensions, tariff barriers and evolving trade realignments 
remain a key overhang, potentially causing selective 
margin pressure.

and profitability.
COMPANY OVERVIEW
Aarti Industries Limited (‘AIL ’ or ‘the Company’) is a leading 
global 
speciality chemicals company. It is renowned for 
its expertise in benzene and toluene-based derivatives. 
The Company is also a leading manufacturer and exporter 
of speciality chemicals used primarily as performance-
enhancing octane boosters in the energy sector.
Headquartered in Mumbai, India, the Company was 
established in 1984 by first-generation technocrats. Over 
the past four decades, AIL has evolved into a recognised 
‘Global Partner of Choice’. This position is driven by its 
ability to collaborate with global customers across the 
product lifecycle, from concept to commercialisation.
AIL ’s evolution is anchored in the ‘Chemistry of 
Collaboration’. Through integrated, strategic partnerships 
with customers, suppliers, and other partners, the Company 
co-creates solutions, optimises processes, and delivers 
long-term value. This approach enables customised delivery 
capabilities while maintaining cost efficiency.
The Company’s competitive advantage is built on a strong 
foundation of integrated operations, process chemistry 
scale-up expertise, and a strategically distributed network 
of research and development (R&D) and pilot plants. AIL 
ranks 4th globally for approximately 75% of its product 
portfolio, serving over 1,100 customers across more than 
60 countries.
Today, AIL has a significant presence across India, the 
Middle East, North America, Europe, and other international 
markets. The Company offers customised and novel 
delivery solutions, including near-to-plant stock points, to 
support key market requirements.
AIL is recognised as a leader in chlorination, nitration, and 
hydrogenation chemistries. It leverages key raw materials 
to drive innovation and strengthen its position in speciality chemicals. The Company’s core operations are centred on 
key value chains, including Nitro Chloro Benzenes (NCB), 
Dichlorobenzenes (DCB), Phenylenediamines (PDA), and 
Nitro Toluene (NT).
These intermediates support downstream applications 
across agrochemicals, pharmaceuticals, polymers, aFuel 
additives, dyes and pigments. During the year, AIL continued 
its strategic shift from bulk product manufacturing to a 
knowledge-driven, application-led solutions provider. This 
transition reflects the expansion of high-value chemistries 
and deeper customer engagement through chemistry-led 
and R&D-oriented solutions.
Increasingly, AIL is evolving from a product-led organisation 
to a platform-led speciality chemicals company. 
Through integrated chemistry platforms, multipurpose 
manufacturing assets, process development expertise and 
customer co-creation capabilities, the Company is building 
scalable growth engines capable of serving multiple end-
use sectors and application areas. This platform-led 
approach enables faster commercialisation, improved 
asset utilisation and deeper strategic engagement with 
global customers.
AIL further strengthened its position through deeper 
backward integration and improved global supply chain 
resilience. Its portfolio remains anchored in long-term 
contracts with global partners. The Company continues to 
scale its integrated manufacturing platforms through cost-
optimisation initiatives and increased capacity utilisation.
At the same time, AIL is steadily transitioning its portfolio 
towards higher-value speciality and performance chemicals. 
The Company is also actively expanding its presence in 
future-focused application areas, including advanced 
materials, electronic chemicals, advanced polymers, clean 
energy value chains and high-performance speciality 
intermediates. These sectors are expected to benefit 
from structural demand growth driven by digitisation, 
electrification, localisation of supply chains and advanced 
manufacturing investments globally.
AIL ’s manufacturing footprint includes 16 state-of-the-art 
plants, 11 of which are equipped with Zero Liquid Discharge 
(ZLD) capabilities. This reflects the Company’s commitment 
to environmental stewardship alongside industrial scale.
During the year, the Company delivered resilient 
performance despite a volatile external environment. The 
first quarter was impacted by corrections in raw material 
prices and inventory losses. However, AIL achieved a strong 
sequential recovery in the subsequent quarters through 
proactive market rebalancing and disciplined execution.

188 Integrated Annual Report 2025-26KEY VALUE CHAINS AND PRODUCT PORTFOLIO
Benzene Value Chain
Benz
ene derivatives remain the Company’s largest 
revenue drivers and a core pillar of its integrated speciality 
chemicals portfolio. The portfolio includes key benzene-
based derivatives such as Nitro Chloro Benzenes (NCB), 
Di-Chlorobenzenes (DCB), and Phenylenediamines (PDA). 
The chain caters to diversified end-use segments, including 
pharmaceuticals through intermediates such as PNCB and 
MDCB, dyes and pigments through NCBs, and polymers, 
where PDCB plays a critical role.
AIL continues to focus on capacity optimisation and 
operational flexibility. The Company debottlenecked 
DCB capacity from 120 KTPA to 140 KTPA by leveraging 
multipurpose assets to produce derivatives, such as 
chloroanilines, via integrated hydrogenation and nitration 
chemistries. Strategically, the portfolio remains well-
positioned for growth. This is supported by the resumption 
of US volumes following improved India-US trade dynamics 
and rising demand for PDCB within the China EV ecosystem. 
In addition, margin recovery prospects in the NCB chain are 
supported by China’s anti-involution measures, which are 
expected to ease competitive intensity and improve pricing 
discipline.
Toluene Value Chain
The Company entered the Toluene Value Chain by 
commissioning its first plant in Dahej in FY 2017-18. Since 
then, the portfolio has steadily scaled up to become one 
of the core pillars of its integrated speciality chemicals 
business. The value chain is centred on Nitro Toluene (NT) 
and its downstream derivatives.
Growth is further anchored by the commissioning of the 
greenfield Zone IV site, which includes Chlorotoluene and 
downstream process blocks, as well as a Multipurpose Plant 
(MPP). The MPP unit was under commissioning trials in  
Q1 FY 2026-27 and expected to be commercialised in  
FY 2026-27. The broader chlorotoluene and downstream 
process blocks in Zone IV are expected to be commissioned 
in phases during the fiscal year. However, timelines have 
shifted by three to four months due to evolving labour 
availability and geopolitical factors.
To facilitate faster ramp-up, AIL progressively engaged in 
discussions with critical potential customers. Commercial 
momentum is further reinforced through initiatives such 
as providing qualification batches from the recently 
commercialised pilot plant and fast-tracking investments 
for advanced intermediates like PEDA. These initiatives strengthen AIL ’s integration across the toluene value chain 
while enhancing its positioning in high-value agrochemical 
and other speciality chemical applications.
Sulphuric Acid Chain
The Sulphuric Acid value chain and Calcium Chloride 
remain integral to the Company’s integrated operations and 
downstream speciality chemicals portfolio. In FY 2025-26, 
Phase I of the Calcium Chloride plant was commercialised 
in Zone IV. This supports AIL ’s strategy for the effective and 
gainful utilisation of by-products. The initiative also enables 
efficient material utilisation, deeper process integration, and 
the adoption of low-cost, novel technologies that enhance 
overall competitiveness.

BUSINESS-WISE PERFORMANCE
Energy 
AIL
’s energy business, primarily driven by Mono Methyl 
Aniline (MMA), continued as a key growth engine. Volumes 
remained strong, supported by sustained demand for fuel 
blending and favourable feedstock spreads. In FY 2025-26, 
the energy segment accounted for 43% of total revenue as 
compared to 36% in the previous year. Over the long term, 
this business is expected to account for 30-40% of the 
Company’s overall business. 
•  Capacity Ramp-up:  In FY 2025-26, capacity was 
scaled up to 290 KTPA (from 200 KTPA). Further scale-up to 360 KTPA is underway and is expected to 
be commissioned in the near term, in line with market 
requirements, providing further momentum for volume 
growth. 
•  Market Diversification: While the US market remained 
important, the Company focused on developing 
alternative markets in Europe and Africa, anticipating 
that the business’s structural strength would enable 
steady margin expansion.  
Agrochemicals
Following the end of a prolonged inventory destocking 
cycle, the agrochemicals segment showed signs of a stable 
recovery in FY 2025-26. While volumes remained stable for 
most of the year, notable growth was witnessed in NT and 
the downstream ethylation chain of products, while pricing 
remained subdued due to competitive pressures from 
China.   
•  Strategic Partnerships: AIL secured a USD 150 
million medium-term supply contract with a global 
agrochemical major in March 2026, for a critical 
intermediate used in crop protection formulations, 
marking a significant milestone in long-term 
collaborative growth. The contract extends to March 
2030 and would be met with existing capacities    
•  Forward Integration:  The PEDA project, a forward 
integration ethylation project at Zone IV is under 
commissioning trials, with a capacity of 4,000 TPA, 
strengthening India’s agrochemical self-reliance and 
providing AIL with a significant cost advantage  
Dyes, Pigments, and Printing Inks
Demand in this segment remained steady throughout the 
year, with volumes expected to improve as global demand 
for textiles and printing revives. However, one of the core 
products, 3,3-DCBH, continued to face global demand

by higher raw material costs and elevated freight rates. The 
impact is expected to be partly offset by improving demand 
in the Indian market. Applications across dyes, pigments, 
and printing inks continued to generate steady cash flows, 
supported by a refined pricing strategy that balanced 
volume growth with margin preservation.  
Polymers and Additives
PDCB demand grew due to its application in the EV sector, 
even as the polymers segment experienced mixed trends.

the US market. This prompted the Company to respond

BUSINESS HIGHLIGHTS
FY 2025-26 marked a year of steady strategic progress for 
AIL 
despite a volatile global environment characterised 
by geopolitical tensions, supply chain disruptions, raw 
material volatility and sustained competitive pressures. The 
Company continued to strengthen its long-term positioning 
through capacity expansion, medium to long-term contracts, 
backward integration initiatives and portfolio diversification 
into higher-value speciality chemicals.
A key strategic milestone was a ₹ 200-250 Crs backwards-
integration capex initiative with a global customer, aimed 
at strengthening integration for the key product under the 
residual 15-year long-term contract structure. 
Another one is the USD 150 million supply agreement with 
a global agrochemical innovator, extending through March 
2030, which enhances long-term revenue visibility without 
incremental capex. 
The Company secured long-term methanol and toluene 
feedstock contracts across GCC and Southeast Asia, 
improving raw material security and cost predictability, and 
entered a strategic chlorine supply partnership with DCM 
Shriram Limited to support its Zone IV Jhagadia facility 
through dedicated pipeline infrastructure.
The Company also advanced its portfolio expansion 
through partnerships, including the exclusive PCBTF 
distribution agreement with Actylis. It further progressed 
joint ventures, including Augene (Superform JV) and the 
recycling-focused Re Aarti platform, all of which remain on 
track for commissioning in FY 27.
From a segment perspective, agrochemicals and pharma 
remained stable in volume but continued to face margin 
pressure due to global oversupply and Chinese competition. 
Among Polymers, EV-linked demand remained a strong 
contributor to growth, while dyes and pigments were 
relatively stable, supported by resilient domestic demand.
Capex during FY 2025-26 stood at about ₹ 1,125 Crs, 
primarily directed towards Zone IV expansion and fast-track 
capacity additions such as MMA, DCB and PEDA-related 
initiatives. This reflects the tail end of a high-investment 
cycle, with management indicating a transition towards lower capex intensity in FY 2026-27 as major projects near 
completion.
Zone IV remained the flagship growth platform, with the 
Calcium Chloride unit commercialised and ramping up, 
while other blocks, including the multipurpose plant and 
PEDA, progressed through commissioning stages, albeit 
with short-term delays, supporting the shift towards higher-
value product streams.
FINANCIAL PERFORMANCE
FY 2025-26 was marked by a challenging operating 
environment characterised by raw material volatility, 
geopolitical disruptions, elevated freight costs, logistics 
bottlenecks and continued competitive pressure from 
Chinese suppliers. Uncertainty relating to US tariffs on  
Indian chemical exports and broader supply chain disruptions  
also weighed on industry conditions during the year.  
Despite this backdrop, the Company delivered a 
resilient performance with revenue rising 12% YoY to  
₹ 9,018 Crs, supported by volume growth, improving 
capacity utilisation, recovery in export volumes, and stable 
domestic demand. Additionally, higher-margin, value-added 
products contributed to overall growth.
EBITDA increased over 15% YoY to ₹ 1,172 Crs, driven by 
operating leverage, cost optimisation initiatives, and scale 
benefits from higher utilisation. Profitability was partly 
impacted by inventory valuation losses, shipment-related 
disruptions, and one-time labour code implementation 
costs of ₹ 15 Crs, though efficiency gains supported gradual 
improvement through the year. The increasing share 
of long-term customer engagements and collaborative 
business models is expected to enhance revenue visibility 
and support margin stability over the medium term.
Finance costs noted accounting adjustments. FY 2025-26 
saw mixed forex impacts, including gains of ~₹ 16 Crs (Q1) 
and ~₹ 10 Crs (Q4), offset by a ₹ 34 Crs mark-to-market 
loss on ECBs (Q2) and a ₹ 39 Crs revaluation loss on an 
unhedged foreign currency loan (Q4). These are non-
cash accounting impacts, highlighting the natural hedge 
provided by the Company’s export profile over the long-term 
repayment cycle. Depreciation remained as expected, with 
potential tax-efficiency benefits as new capacities come 
online.
PAT for FY 2025-26 increased 27% YoY to ₹ 419 Crs, 
supported by stronger operating performance and 
improved leverage, despite forex-related impacts and other 
exceptional items.

Capital Expenditure
FY 2025-26 capex stood at ₹ 1,125 Crs, marking the peak 
phase of investment in the Zone IV platform development. 
During the year, key assets such as the calcium chloride 
plant, multipurpose plant (MPP), 4,000 TPA PEDA facility, 
and related downstream units advanced through various 
commissioning stages. However, execution timelines 
were delayed by 3-4 months due to labour constraints, 
commercial LPG availability issues, and election-related 
workforce migration. As a result, while the calcium chloride 
plant has completed commercial runs and is currently 
ramping up, the MPP and PEDA facilities continue to 
undergo commissioning trials.
For FY 2026-27, capex is expected to moderate to ₹ 750-
800 Crs as the Company shifts from a heavy investment 
phase towards optimisation and execution-led growth. 
The Zone IV platform, forming part of a total build-out of  
₹ 1,600-1,800 Crs, is now entering its revenue-generation 
phase. Initial commercial revenue aggregation from these 
assets is expected to commence in the second half of  
FY 2026-27. Thereafter, revenue contribution is likely to 
increase gradually as operations stabilise and utilisation 
levels improve.BUSINESS OUTLOOK
The near-term outlook is expected to benefit from improved 
capacity 
utilisation, healthy visibility of long-term contracts 
and continued execution of integration-led initiatives. The 
Company expects gradual deleveraging, with net debt likely 
to moderate this year through operating improvements and 
sustained efficiency measures. Margin expansion is also 
expected to be supported by operating leverage and cost 
optimisation initiatives.
For FY 2026-27, the capex cycle is expected to enter a 
low-intensity phase, with spending projected to decline 
significantly to well below ₹ 1,000 Crs due to the absence 
of major greenfield projects. The effective tax rate is 
also expected to normalise within the 9-15% range. 
Operationally, key milestones include commissioning the 
Zone IV facilities during FY 2026-27, with initial revenue 
contributions expected in the second half of the year, as 
well as commissioning the JVs. Additional support may 
also arise from external demand-supply dynamics, including 
potential benefits from shifts in the Chinese chemical 
market, beginning FY 2026-27.
Aarti Industries is steadily shifting its portfolio towards 
higher-margin, innovation-led segments, with greater focus 
on advanced materials and speciality chemistries, while 
reducing dependence on commoditised bulk chemicals. 
This transition is being strengthened through deeper CDMO 
engagement, including multiple early-stage collaborations 
with global innovators. R&D efforts remain focused on 
advanced materials, polymer science and emerging 
application areas, supported by AI-led tools and digital 
manufacturing initiatives to improve process efficiency, 
energy intensity and operational reliability.
Alongside this strategic evolution, the Company has 
strengthened its ESG and people credentials. It received an 
EcoVadis platinum rating (Top 1%) and was included in the 
CDP – A List for climate performance. The Company also 
recently won the Gallup Exceptional Workplace Award 2026, 
becoming one of the first Indian manufacturing companies 
to receive this recognition. Collectively, these achievements 
reflect the Company’s growing focus on sustainability, 
governance quality and organisational capability, alongside 
its ongoing business transformation.

Risk Category Risk Description Mitigation and Strategic Response
Trade and Tariffs The impact of US tariffs on Indian chemical 
exports is creating pricing pressure and eroding 
competitiveness against European and Chinese

Africa

and engaging in proactive customer 
renegotiations

rerouting, port congestion at Kandla, and 
intermittent production at the Kutch facility•  Demonstration of commercial agility 
with swift redirection of trade flows 
•  Maintenance of higher inventory stocks 
(1.5 to 2 months) of key raw materials 
like aniline for production security
Competitive Intensity Intense pricing pressure and hyper-competition 
from China, particularly in agrochemicals, 
pharmaceuticals, and fluoro products•  Use of indigenous technology to become 
a lowest-cost producer 
•  Shift in focus from bulk products to high-
value, application-led advanced materials
•  Ongoing monitoring of China’s anti-
innovation policy and removal of VAT 
export rebates
Raw Material Volatility Steep corrections in input prices (benzene and 
aniline), leading to inventory valuation losses 
and pricing volatility across the value chain•  Implementation of new pricing formulas 
in long-term raw material contracts 
•  Deployment of AI and digital tools for 
real-time process control and production 
optimisation to maintain cost leadership

 Leadership Transition
 The Company has undertaken a leadership transition 
with effect from October 01, 2026, as part of its long-
term succession planning and its continuing endeavour 
to strengthen governance, institutional leadership and 
sustainable value creation. The transition is aimed at 
further embedding a professional management-led 
operating model, while continuing to benefit from the 
strategic guidance and extensive industry experience 
of the Promoter Directors.
 Consequent to the leadership transition, the Executive 
Directors from the promoter category, namely; Shri

01, 2026, subject to the approval of the Members in

 The leadership transition marks the next phase in the 
evolution of the Company, with professional executive 
management taking responsibility for the day-to-day 
operations and strategic execution of the Company, 
while the Promoter Directors continue to provide 
strategic guidance and oversight.
 The transition does not entail any change in the 
Company’s long-term strategic direction. The 
Company remains focused on disciplined execution, 
customer-centric innovation, operational excellence 
and sustainable growth, while continuing to strengthen 
its position as a trusted global partner of choice in the 
specialty chemicals industry.

10. ANNUAL PERFORMANCE EVALUATION
 The Company has a structured assessment process. 
The 
evaluations are carried out in a confidential manner 
and each member of the Board provides his/her 
feedback by rating based on various metrics. Feedback 
is collected through a structured questionnaire. 
 Two-Layer Annual Performance Evaluation Process
 The Company maintains a structured, formal process 
for the annual performance evaluation of the Board, 
its Committees, individual Directors and the Chairman 
of the Company. This comprehensive exercise is 
guided by criteria laid down by the Nomination and 
=== page 103 ===
200 Integrated Annual Report 2025-26Remuneration Committee (“NRC”) and is conducted 
through a confidential, structured questionnaire across 
various metrics.
 The evaluation is rigorously executed through a two-
layer process to ensure objective assessment and 
compliance with regulatory mandates:
1. First Layer (Independent Directors’ 
Meeting-IDM): The Independent Directors review 
the collective performance of the Board, the Non-
Independent Directors, and the Chairman of the 
Company.
2. Second Layer (Board of Directors - BoD):  The 
Board evaluates the performance of the Board 
itself, its various Committees and all individual 
Directors.
 Key Outcomes for FY 2025–26
 The performance review for the Financial Year 2025-
26 confirmed the Board’s high level of effectiveness, 
with an overall average rating consistently exceeding 
3.7 (out of 4.0). The evaluation highlighted:
 •  Governance Strength: Unanimous agreement 
on the Board’s integrity, legal obligations, and 
collective responsibility, all scoring a perfect 
4.0. The Chairman received perfect scores 
(4.0/4.0) across all respondents, reflecting  
strong leadership.

14. VIGIL MECHANISM/WHISTLE BLOWER POLICY 
 The Company maintains a robust Vigil Mechanism 
and 
Whistleblower Policy, facilitating the confidential 
reporting of genuine concerns related to unethical 
conduct, actual or suspected fraud, potential leakage 
of Unpublished Price Sensitive Information (UPSI) and 
violations of the Company’s Code of Conduct.
 Reporting channels include a dedicated Ethics Officer 
and a newly launched Hotline number. To ensure 
impartiality, complaints against the Ethics Officer 
are escalated to the Chairman of the Company, and those against the Chairman are referred to the Audit 
Committee Chairperson. All reported grievances 
undergo thorough and objective investigation.
 Comprehensive safeguards are strictly enforced to 
protect whistleblowers and assist employees from 
any form of discrimination, harassment, victimisation, 
or unfair employment practices. Confidentiality 
is paramount; the Ethics Officer does not issue 
acknowledgments to protect the individual’s identity, 
and the identities of both the whistleblower and the 
subject are maintained with the highest degree of 
secrecy throughout the investigation process. For 
exceptional cases requiring elevated protection 
against victimisation, direct access to the Chairman of 
the Audit Committee is provided.
 Ethical governance is institutionalised through the 
mandatory Aarti Online Training Module (ATOMs), 
a key component of onboarding and compliance. 
This programme ensures that all new employees are 
aligned with our ethical standards from the outset, 
equipping the workforce to effectively identify, report 
and mitigate potential governance risks.
 The Company formally affirms that no request for 
access to the Audit Committee Chairperson was 
denied during the year under review.
 The said policy has been posted on the website of 
the Company and the web link thereto is: https://

28. RISK MANAGEMENT 
 The Company has established a robust Enterprise Risk 
Management 
(ERM) framework in line with applicable 
regulatory requirements. The framework enables 
the identification, assessment, and mitigation of 
risks across key functions - Commercial, Operations, 
Finance, Human Resources, Information Systems, 
Technology, Research & Development and Expansion. 
A centralised Risk Register ensures that risks 
identified by Risk Owners are systematically recorded, 
monitored and escalated through a well-defined  
governance structure.
 To strengthen risk prioritisation, the Company utilises 
a Risk Profile Heat Map, which evaluates risks 
based on their likelihood and impact, classifying 
them into Critical, Major, Moderate, Minor and 
Insignificant categories. These are further aligned 
with the Company’s risk appetite and grouped into 
High, Medium and Low buckets, enabling focused 
monitoring of critical risks and effective allocation of 
mitigation resources.
 During the year under review, key risks included 
competitive intensity, margin pressures, supply chain 
disruptions and potential impacts from natural events. 
The Company addressed these through enhanced 
process capabilities, optimised asset utilisation and 
robust internal controls supported by well-defined 
Board’s Report FS CO
205 Aarti Industries Limitedstandard operating procedures, ensuring operational 
continuity and resilience.
 The Company also remained vigilant to emerging 
external risks such as changes in foreign trade policies 
and evolving geopolitical developments that impact 
global supply chains. These risks were continuously 
monitored and integrated into the Company’s Business 
Continuity Planning and strategic decision-making 
processes.
 The Risk Management framework is overseen by the 
Risk Management Committee and reviewed by the 
Board to ensure its effectiveness and alignment with 
the evolving business environment. The Board is of the 
opinion that the Company’s risk management systems 
are adequate and effective, with no material risks 
identified that may threaten the Company’s continuity.

 Safety stands as AIL ’s non-negotiable foundation,

 FY 2025-26 was marked by the significant progression

initiative has enhanced the tools like BBSO (Behaviour 
Based safety Observation), PTW (Permit to Work), JCC

as Condition Listening (CL), Safety Action Meetings 
(SAM), Personal Safety Action Plans (PSAP) and Mera

floor teams to further strengthen our safety culture. 
- BBSO & SAM: Empower teams to identify 
unsafe conditions and proactively eliminate 
repetitive unsafe acts through deeper employee 
engagement.
- Condition Listening (CL): Drives hazard 
elimination and advances plant maintenance as 
a critical operational component.
- PSAPs & ‘Mera Plant Mera Abhiman’: Cultivate 
personal safety accountability from leadership to 
the associate workforce, creating a closed safety 
loop that ensures operational excellence.
 Through Unnati 2.0, the Company upgraded safety 
digital infrastructure by migrating critical tools (BBSO, 
GPC, MOC and DCA) to an enhanced platform. This 
transition delivered substantial value and earned 
positive user feedback. To ensure rigorous oversight, 
company developed sophisticated dashboards that 
significantly strengthen our governance and review 
mechanisms. 
 During FY 2025-26, Company completed two Board-
recommended cycles of quarterly inter-business

31. ENVIRONMENT
 The Company is committed to advancing 
envir
onmental stewardship by embedding robust 
environmental management practices, strengthening 
climate resilience, and promoting responsible 
resource utilisation across its operations. Through a 
structured Environmental and Waste Management 
framework, we continuously enhance operational 
efficiency while minimising our environmental 
footprint and dependence on natural resources. Water 
stewardship and advanced effluent management 
remain key material priorities, supported by 
continuous investments in process optimisation 
and resource recovery initiatives. These efforts have 
delivered measurable environmental outcomes, 
including improved effluent quality, enhanced resource 
efficiency, and the transformation of waste streams 
into value-added products, reinforcing our commitment 
to circularity and sustainable operations.
 Water Stewardship
 Recognising water as a critical natural resource, 
Company continues to strengthen its water stewardship 
practices by embedding circular water management 
across its operations. Our comprehensive 3R (Reduce, 
Reuse and Recycle) strategy, supported by a long-term 
vision of achieving Zero Liquid Discharge (ZLD) across 
all manufacturing facilities, enables us to optimise 
freshwater consumption while enhancing operational 
resilience. During FY 2025–26, we expanded our water 
conservation initiatives through enhanced rainwater 
Board’s Report FS CO
207 Aarti Industries Limitedharvesting, increased recovery of MEE and steam 
condensate, 
and higher utilisation of treated sewage 
water and RO permeate. As a result of these sustained 
efforts, eight manufacturing facilities have achieved 
ZLD status and three facilities are ZLD-ready, with 
the remaining sites advancing towards ZLD through 
phased implementation and continuous infrastructure 
enhancements.
 Air Quality and Emission Management
 Company is committed to maintaining high standards 
of air quality management through a proactive 
and technology-driven approach to emission 
control. Advanced pollution abatement systems, 
including wet and dry scrubbers, bag filters, and 
Electrostatic Precipitators (ESPs), are deployed across 
manufacturing facilities to effectively manage process 
and flue gas emissions. Continuous investments 
in process innovation, including dry scrubber 
systems with lime dosing technology, have further 
enhanced sulphur dioxide (SO2) emission reduction. 
Complementing these efforts, comprehensive Leak 
Detection and Repair (LDAR) programmes minimise 
fugitive emissions and volatile organic compounds 
(VOCs), strengthening operational integrity and 
environmental performance.
 Real-time environmental monitoring is enabled through 
Continuous Emission Monitoring Systems (CEMS) and 
online hazardous gas detection systems installed 
across manufacturing sites, with direct integration 
to CPCB and SPCB regulatory portals to ensure 
regulatory compliance and operational transparency. 
Through these sustained efforts, ambient air quality 
is consistently maintained in accordance with the 
National Ambient Air Quality Standards (NAAQS). 
The Company has also completely phased out Ozone 
Depleting Substances (ODS) and confirms that no 
Persistent Organic Pollutants (POPs), as defined under 
the Stockholm Convention, are generated through its 
operations, reinforcing its commitment to responsible 
environmental stewardship and sustainable 
manufacturing.
 Waste Management and Circularity
 Waste management at Company is anchored in the 
principles of circularity and responsible resource 
stewardship. Our integrated waste management 
strategy is built on three strategic priorities—source 
reduction, resource recovery through the 4R principle (Reuse, Recover, Recycle and Reprocess), and 
environmentally sound disposal. By prioritising co-
processing and other resource recovery pathways over 
conventional landfilling and incineration, we maximise 
waste valorisation while advancing our circular 
economy objectives.
 In FY 2025–26, we diverted 95% of waste away 
from landfill and 13/16 divisions are certified as 
Zero Waste to Landfill. We also enhanced our waste 
governance through the digitalisation of hazardous 
waste monitoring and round-the-clock tracking of 
waste transportation vehicles via the Aarti Logistics 
Control Centre. These initiatives strengthen end-to-
end traceability, improve regulatory compliance, and 
reinforce our commitment to transparent, safe, and 
responsible waste management practices.

37.  INTERNAL CONTROL SYSTEMS AND THEIR 
ADEQU
ACY
 During the year under review, the Company strengthened 
its 
Internal Audit framework by transitioning to a 
Hybrid Internal Audit Model, combining its in-house 
audit function with the appointment of M/s. Protiviti, 
Global Business Consulting Firm as its external 
support to bring more effectiveness to the overall  
audit framework.
 This transition reflects the Company’s commitment 
to strengthen governance standards and was 
undertaken with the objective of driving tangible 
value by leveraging global best practices to enhance 
the depth, quality, and actionable insights of audit 
outcomes, while also improving process efficiency 
using specialised expertise.
 The internal audit department prepares an annual 
audit plan and prioritises audit activities based on 
the criticality of system/process gaps. Reviews 
are conducted on an ongoing basis based on a comprehensive risk-based audit plan, which is 
approved by the Audit Committee at the beginning 
of each year. The Internal Audit team reviews and 
reports to the management and the Audit Committee 
about compliance with internal controls, and the 
efficiency and effectiveness of operations as well as 
the key process risks. The Audit Committee meets 
every quarter to review and discuss the Internal Audit 
reports, follow up on action plans of past significant 
audit issues Internal financial control systems of the 
Company are commensurate with size and the nature 
of its operations of the Company. 
 Internal Financial Controls have been designed to 
provide reasonable assurance with regard to recording 
and providing reliable financial and operational 
information, complying with applicable accounting 
standards and relevant statutes, safeguarding assets 
from unauthorised use, executing transactions with 
proper authorisation and ensuring compliance of 
corporate policies. Statutory Auditors Report on 
Internal Financial Controls as required under Clause (i) 
of sub-section 3 of Section 143 of the Companies Act, 
2013 is annexed with the Independent Auditors’ Report.
38.  AUDIT COMMITTEE OVERSIGHT AND DEEP DIVE 
SESSION
S
 In alignment with our commitment to maintaining 
the highest standards of corporate governance and 
proactive risk management, the Audit Committee, 
during the financial year under review, instituted 
periodic “Deep Dive” Sessions as a strategic extension 
to its regular calendar meetings.
 Recognizing that the evolving macroeconomic, 
regulatory, and technological landscapes require 
a more granular layer of scrutiny, these dedicated 
sessions were introduced to facilitate enlarged, 
uninterrupted deliberation on complex and high-
impact risk domains. Unlike routine meetings focused 
on compliance checklists and financial approvals, the 
Deep Dive framework enables the Committee to:
 •  Enhance Risk Scrutiny: Evaluate the root 
causes, operational vulnerabilities, and  
long-term implications of systemic risks facing 
the Company.
 •  Engage Directly with Experts: Foster direct, 
open dialogue with operational heads, internal 
auditors, and external subject matter experts on 
specialised topics.
=== page 108 ===
210 Integrated Annual Report 2025-26 •  Strengthen Internal Controls: Review the 
agility and adequacy of existing internal control 
frameworks against emerging threats before they 
impact financial reporting.
 These initiatives have significantly strengthened the 
Committee’s oversight capabilities, delivering deeper 
assurance and strategic resilience to the organisation.
39.  ENGAGEMENT WITH THOSE CHARGED WITH 
GO
VERNANCE (“TCWG”)
 Effective corporate governance relies heavily on a 
tr
ansparent, constructive and independent relationship 
between Management, Internal Audit, the Statutory 
Auditors and Those Charged With Governance (TCWG).
 Under Paragraph 11 of SA 260 (Revised), read with 
circular  no. NF-25013/3/2025--NFRA issued by 
National Financial Reporting Authority (NFRA), M/s 
Gokhale & Sathe, Statutory Auditors of the Company, 
determined the entire ‘Board of Directors’ as Those 
Charged With Governance (TCWG) and then the Board 
appointed the CEO as the ‘Nodal Person’ on behalf of 
the Board (TCWG) to enable effective implementation 
of the standards SA 260 on an overall communication 
framework between the TCWG and the Auditors. 
 Bringing the circular into effect from April 01, 2026, 
formal interactions were conducted, TCWG met twice 
on April 03, 2026 and April 30, 2026 to deliberate on 
critical matters, including:
 •  Audit Planning and Scope: Reviewing the overall 
audit strategy, identifying key risk areas, and 
determining material thresholds prior to the 
commencement of the audit.
 •  Significant Findings & Key Audit Matters (KAMs): 
Engaging in rigorous discussions regarding 
complex accounting estimates, judgments made 
by management and the qualitative aspects of 
the Company’s financial reporting.
 •  Internal Control Observations: Addressing 
any deficiencies or areas of improvement 
identified by the auditors within the internal 
control environment, along with management’s 
subsequent remediation plans.
 •  Auditor Independence: Confirming and reviewing 
the independence, objectivity and effectiveness 
of the audit process.
 The continuous, structured dialogue between the 
Statutory Auditors and TCWG ensures robust checks and 
balances, reinforcing the credibility of the Company’s 
financial disclosures and governance mechanism s.40. SECRETARIAL STANDARDS COMPLIANCE

A)  CONSERVATION FOR ENERGY AND REDUCTION IN 
CARBON EMISSION
 The Steps Taken or Impact on Conservation  of Energy;
 
 To achieve our emission reduction targets validated 
by Science Based Targets initiative (SBTi),  our 
multi-disciplinary teams operate through a strategic 
framework anchored by three fundamental pillars: 
Fit for Purpose, Focus to Finish, and Right First Time. 
Our decarbonization roadmap focuses on high-impact 
initiatives such as mitigating energy losses, optimizing 
equipment performance, and refining process 
efficiencies. We are actively transitioning toward 
renewable power sources and alternative fuels while 
integrating cutting-edge technologies to eliminate 
process-related emissions.
  These efforts are supported by a granular approach 
to energy conservation, including the synchronization 
of energy demand and supply, the implementation of 
energy-efficient maintenance protocols, and the use 
of modern monitoring devices to reduce equipment 
idle time. Central to our energy governance is a digital 
Energy Management System (EnMS). This IT-driven 
platform tracks critical electrical metrics and produces 
automated, bespoke reporting, delivering the real-
time insights necessary for agile and effective energy 
management.
  Key energy-saving measures implemented during 
FY 2025-26 across utilities and process systems 
to improve efficiency and reliability are installation 
of VFDs on high-load equipment, performance 
improvement and replacement of water chillers, and 
extensive pump upgrades across cooling water and 
chilled water systems. 
  Additional steps such as impeller modifications to 
avoid throttling, installation of pressure transmitters, 
and new pump installations have optimized system 
performance. Integration and interlocking of chillers, 
pumps, and air compressors further ensured operation 
based on demand, reducing energy wastage. We have 
reduced power consumption by approximately 2.4 
million kWh during FY 2025–26.
  Through process optimization we have recovered 
28,96,712 GJ of steam from the distillation condenser 
during 2025-26, this is an increase of 77% from the 
previous FY. We have regularized usage of Biomass 
for replacing coal gradually in order to reduce carbon 
emissions.   Furthermore we have started usage Bio-ethanol 
on a regular mode to move towards elimination of 
conventional liquid fuels
  AIL has commissioned a group captive hybrid 
renewable energy plant for sourcing 13.2 MW of 
renewable power in FY 2023–24, with an investment of 
₹15.18 crore. During the current financial year, AIL has 
reduced approximately 37,000 tCO2e using renewable 
electricity from this 13.2 MW hybrid plant.
  Further, the Board of AIL has approved Phase-II 
expansion of 25.7 MW hybrid renewable capacity in  
FY 2024-25, out of this 7.9 MW is already commissioned 
and we are receiving electricity from it. We expect 
that the remaining 17.8 MW will be commissioned in 
FY27. Further as part of Phase-III 2.75 MW of wind 
power is being received from November 2025 and we 
have reduced more than 400 tCO2e using renewable 
electricity from this project. Once all the phases are 
commissioned we will be meeting more than 68% of 
our electricity requirements from renewable sources. 
  We estimate to reduce more than 100,000 mt tCO2e 
through these initiatives in coming FY.
  The following are the major steps taken during FY 
2025-26 to conserve energy:
	•  Zone 1: 
		   Installation of VFD’s and linking their speed 
variations to relevant process parameters
		   Optimizing usage of air compressor in acid 
and organic divisions
		  Replacement and refurbishment of pumps 
		   Avoiding flow throttling by reducing flow 
speed through VFD, by replacing impeller etc
		   Power saving  in ETP by replacing surface 
aeration with diffused aeration for existing 
blowers 
		  Revamping the RO to reducing MEE load
		   Increasing power generation from CPP by 
creating additional infrastructure
		   Energy saving through performance 
improvement and optimization of water 
chilling plant in Topaz division
	•  Zone 2:
		   Installation of new VAM chiller and 
transitioning from a fixed point to a dew 
point based timer controller.

B)  TECHNOLOGY ABSORPTION, ADAPTATION, AND 
INNOVATION
  Efforts made towards technology Absorption, 
Adaptation and Inno
vation:
  Our focused efforts in technology absorption, 
adaptation, and innovation are integral to enhancing 
operational efficiency, optimising resource 
utilisation, and driving sustainable growth across our 
manufacturing landscape. We are leveraging cutting-
edge technologies to fundamentally reshape our 
processes, ensuring that technological excellence 
serves as the bedrock of our environmental 
stewardship.
 1.   Technology Absorption: Establishing 
Foundations for Decarbonization
   Technological absorption involves the strategic 
integration of advanced tools and methodologies 
that establish a data-driven framework for 
sustainability and resource optimization.
		•   Carbon Footprint Intelligence (Gabi 
Software): We are implementing the Gabi 
software platform to calculate the carbon 
footprint thereby successfully completing 
the baseline calculation for all Zone 4 
chlorinated molecules. This initiative 
provides critical data for targeted carbon 
mitigation strategies at our new upcoming 
location. In addition to this we are using 
the Gabi software for identifying carbon 
mitigation strategies for our existing 
locations also.
		•   Enhanced Resource Efficiency:  By 
strategically increasing Efficiency for Reaction 
from 85% to 90%, we are directly reducing the overall carbon footprint associated with the 
manufacturing process.
 2.  Strategic Adaptation: Pioneering Resource 
Circularity and Carbon Mitigation
   Strategic adaptation focuses on optimizing 
existing infrastructure through innovative 
engineering to achieve immediate, measurable 
environmental benefits and establish closed-loop 
systems.
		•  Carbon Mitigation and Energy Savings (Cold 
Hot Oil Circulation Manufacturing plant): The 
implemented scheme delivers substantial 
environmental returns, estimated to achieve 
an annual reduction of approximately 10,867  
tonnes of CO2 emissions. It also secured 
significant resource optimization through 
a 20% reduction in LSHS fuel consumption 
and reductions in Raw Material-1 (5.29%) 
and Raw Material-2 (0.57%).
 3.   Disruptive Innovation:  The Future of Green 
Chemistry and Safety
   Innovation is focused on developing and 
implementing next-generation manufacturing 
technologies that fundamentally enhance 
process safety and productivity while minimizing 
physical footprint.
	  •  Zero-Inventory Safety (Batch process 
to Flow Reaction - Pinch Tube Reactor): 
Transitioning nucleophilic substitution 
from batch to a pinch tube reactor reduced 
residence time from 5 hours to 9 minutes, 
significantly lowering energy consumption, 
minimizing waste generation, and enhancing 
the sustainability of the manufacturing 
process. 
	  •  Poly oil:  Our plastic pyrolysis project 
reflects our commitment to sustainability by 
converting ~9,000 tonnes of plastic waste 
annually (25 TPD) into valuable resources, 
preventing landfilling and open burning. 
By enabling circular use of materials and 
reducing reliance on conventional waste 
disposal, the project delivers measurable 
environmental benefits and supports long-
term decarbonization goals. 
 Benefits Derived as a result of above efforts:
 •  Achieve lower overall project costs for the 
expansion initiative.
 •  Implement strategies to significantly reduce 
production expenditures (Opex).
 •  Proactively minimize carbon emissions, waste 
streams, and liquid effluent.

GO
VERNANCE
At Aarti Industries Limited (AIL), Corporate Governance 
goes 
beyond the regulatory compliances — it serves as 
the strategic bedrock for sustainable, inclusive growth. 
Anchored by our core values of Care, Integrity, and 
Excellence, our governance framework actively drives 
accountability, agility, and long-term value creation. We 
are steadfast in our commitment to the highest global 
standards, fostering a Board-driven approach built on 
robust policies, ethical codes, and forward-looking 
practices. By prioritising sustainability, ethical leadership, 
and collaborative success, we reinforce our vision of being 
the “Global Partner of Choice” while making a profoundly 
positive socioeconomic impact.In pursuit of our theme of ‘Perform to Transform,’ governance 
at AIL has evolved from a traditional compliance mandate 
into a proactive, strategic approach influenced by several 
key global trends:
• Global economic trends and regulatory changes: The 
Company is actively aligning its framework with broad 
economic shifts, changing regulatory landscapes, and 
evolving global best practices.
• Elevated investor expectations: The Company’s 
governance evolution is directly influenced by shifting 
demands and expectations from its investors.
• Growing emphasis on ethical business conduct:  There 
is a heightened global focus on ethical leadership, 
responsible business practices, and sustainability.
Driven by these trends, AIL has significantly broadened its 
governance scope beyond traditional financial performance. 
The strategy now heavily integrates Environmental, Social, 
and Governance (ESG) metrics, Board diversity, shareholders 
empowerment, independent oversight and enhanced data 
transparency. Ultimately, these global movements are 
pushing the Company to utilise corporate governance as 
a dynamic force for operational resilience and sustainable 
value creation.

BOARD OF DIRECTORS
Composition as on March 31, 2026
As 
of March 31, 2026, the Company’s Board of Directors 
comprises an optimal composition of 14 seasoned 
professionals, structured to ensure strategic oversight and 
stringent regulatory compliance. This constitution includes 
six executive Directors and eight non-executive Directors - 
seven of whom serve in an Independent capacity—thereby 
satisfying the statutory mandates of Section 149(4) of the 
Companies Act, 2013, alongside Regulations 17(1)(a) and 
17(1)(b) of the Listing Regulations. This deliberate structural 
balance reinforces independent governance, mitigates 
conflicts of interest, and aligns corporate oversight.
Emphasising the material value of Boardroom diversity, the 
Company strictly adheres to all regulatory requirements 
regarding the appointment of Women Directors, viewing 
gender diversity as an integral component of progressive 
corporate governance that drives multi-dimensional 
decision-making. To sustain this efficacy, the Board 
strategically balances deep institutional knowledge with 
contemporary market insights by maintaining a healthy 
mix of long-serving and newly appointed Directors. This 
nuanced tenure profile ensures the organisation remains 
highly adaptable to evolving strategic priorities while firmly 
preserving its foundational corporate memory.
Operational continuity and systematic Board refreshment 
are governed by a structured framework under which one-third of the eligible rotational Directors are evaluated for 
reappointment annually. Furthermore, the continuation of 
all Board members is rigorously linked to the outcomes of a 
comprehensive annual performance evaluation process. By 
systematically assessing individual effectiveness, strategic 
alignment, and ongoing contributions, this appraisal 
framework reinforces absolute accountability and ensures 
the maintenance of a high-performing, forward-looking 
governing body.
